question: What happens when Redis goes down?
answer_hinglish:
API serve karta rehta hai, lekin kuch protections temporarily off ho jaati hain -- yeh deliberate 'fail open' design hai. Component by component: (1) Cache (`TenantCache.get_or_load`): `RedisError` pe seedha `loader()` -- har request DB se tenant aur role padhegi. Latency aur DB load badhega, correctness same. `invalidate` errors swallow karta hai. (2) Rate limit (`check_rate`): RedisError pe `return` -- koi 429 nahi; comment 'fail open: availability for paying customers over strict limiting'. (3) Quota (`meter`): RedisError pe `return 0` -- usage count nahi hogi aur quota enforce nahi hoga. (4) Jobs: `enqueue` (LPUSH) pe RedisError catch nahi hai -- `POST /reports` 500 dega, aur report row 'queued' status mein atak jayegi (DB commit ho chuka). Worker ka BRPOP fail -> worker crash/loop error. (5) `/usage` route: review se pehle seedha `redis.get` -> 500; ab RedisError pe `api_calls: null` (unknown) return karta hai. (6) Usage flush -- nahi chalega; Redis data agar lost hua (no persistence) toh last flush ke baad ke counts gaye.

Kya fail closed nahi hona chahiye tha? Trade-off: rate limit abuse protection hai, core functionality nahi; Redis blip pe saare paying customers ko 503 dena business ke liye bura. Lekin is window mein abusive tenant unlimited requests bhej sakta hai -- isliye monitoring zaroori (TRADEOFFS #9: 'monitor it'). Redis client `BlockingConnectionPool(max_connections=50, timeout=2)` hai -- Redis hang ho toh requests 2s tak wait karengi connection ke liye. FAILURE_SCENARIOS #15.
why_needed: Dependency failure behaviour har production design mein poocha jaata hai; fail-open/closed ka conscious choice dikhana zaroori.
real_world_analogy: Mall ka parking counter (Redis) band ho gaya: gate khula chhod do (fail open) taaki customers aayein, lekin guard alert rakho ki koi truck bhar ke na ghus jaye.
how_it_works: RedisError -> cache bypass, rate/quota skip, invalidation skipped, /usage returns null; still-uncaught path (report enqueue) -> 500.
advantages: Core API available during Redis outage
disadvantages: Report enqueue (POST /reports) still 500s when Redis is down
common_mistakes: Har Redis call pe inconsistent handling
follow_up_questions: Kaunse features fail closed hone chahiye?
Redis HA (Sentinel/Cluster) ka plan?
Local fallback rate limiter kaise?

question: What happens when a stolen refresh token is replayed?
answer_hinglish:
Do cases. Case 1: attacker chori kiya hua token victim se PEHLE use karta hai. Attacker ko naya pair mil jaata hai aur purana token revoke. Jab victim ka client apna (ab revoked) token refresh karta hai -> reuse detected -> poori family revoke -> attacker ka naya token bhi dead. Dono logout; victim dobara login karta hai (password chahiye), attacker ke paas password nahi. Case 2: victim pehle refresh kar chuka hai, attacker purana token replay karta hai -> revoked token -> reuse detected -> family revoke, including victim ka current token. Attacker ko kuch nahi mila, victim logout -- inconvenience, lekin safe.

Dono cases mein attacker ki access window: maximum ek access token lifetime (15 min) agar Case 1 mein usne pehle refresh kiya -- aur woh access token family revoke ke baad bhi expiry tak valid rahega (stateless JWT). Yeh documented gap hai.

`test_auth_flow_and_refresh_rotation_with_reuse_detection` Case 2 chalata hai: login -> tok; refresh -> r1; purana `tok.refresh_token` replay -> 401 with 'reuse' in message; ab `r1.refresh_token` bhi 401. FAILURE_SCENARIOS #7.

Kya nahi hota: user ko notification nahi jaata, reuse event audit/metric mein record nahi hota (sirf exception). Production mein reuse detection security signal hai -- alert, aur shayad saari families revoke (sirf yeh family nahi) kyunki device compromise ho sakta hai.
why_needed: Token theft scenarios security interviews mein standard hain; reuse detection ka exact behaviour batana chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Do log same token number leke counter pe aaye -- counter clerk dono ko wapas bhejta hai aur kehta hai 'ID ke saath naya token lo'. Asli customer ke paas ID (password) hai, chor ke paas nahi.
how_it_works: Revoked token presented -> family_id lookup -> UPDATE all in family revoked -> commit -> 401 'reuse detected'.
code_example:
# real (trimmed) tests/test_api.py
r1 = (await c.post("/auth/refresh", json={"refresh_token": tok["refresh_token"]})).json()
stolen = await c.post("/auth/refresh", json={"refresh_token": tok["refresh_token"]})
assert stolen.status_code == 401 and "reuse" in stolen.json()["error"]["message"]
assert (await c.post("/auth/refresh", json={"refresh_token": r1["refresh_token"]})).status_code == 401
advantages: Theft detected regardless of who uses first
common_mistakes: Reuse pe sirf us token ko reject (family nahi)
follow_up_questions: Reuse detection pe aur kya karoge (alert, revoke all)?
Refresh token binding (DPoP) kya hai?
Access token ko bhi turant kaise maaroge?

question: What happens if the application is compromised and tries to erase or alter the audit trail?
answer_hinglish:
Database mana kar deta hai. App `saas_app` role se connect karta hai jiske paas `audit_logs` pe sirf `SELECT, INSERT` hai. Attacker SQL injection ya stolen app credentials se `UPDATE audit_logs SET action = 'covered-up'` ya `DELETE FROM audit_logs` chalaye -> 'permission denied for table audit_logs'. `test_audit_log_is_append_only_for_the_app` dono assert karta hai. FAILURE_SCENARIOS #6. TRUNCATE privilege bhi grant nahi hai.

Aur kya attacker kar sakta hai? (1) Naye fake audit rows INSERT -- haan, insert allowed hai, toh noise add kar sakta hai (lekin RLS ki wajah se sirf current context ke tenant mein, aur context woh khud set kar sakta hai kyunki app compromise hai). (2) Doosre tables tamper -- haan, app ke paas unpe UPDATE/DELETE hai; lekin unke actions (agar app code se hon) audit hote; raw SQL se kiye gaye changes audit nahi hote kyunki audit app-level insert hai, trigger nahi. (3) Tenant delete -> `audit_logs` `ON DELETE CASCADE`. Review mein yeh gap mila tha: app ke paas `tenants` pe DELETE grant tha, toh `DELETE FROM tenants WHERE id = X` cascade karke us tenant ke audit logs uda deta -- grants ke intent ke khilaaf. Fix: migration 0004 `REVOKE DELETE ON tenants FROM saas_app`; ab tenant deletion sirf privileged process kar sakta hai. Test: `test_app_role_cannot_delete_tenants`. (Alternative jo aur strong hota: audit FK ko RESTRICT ya audit ko alag store.)

Production hardening: audit ko external append-only store (S3 Object Lock, SIEM) mein stream (logical decoding/CDC se), hash chaining, aur DB triggers se audit jo app bypass na kar sake.
why_needed: 'Assume breach' thinking -- audit trail attacker ke against bhi tikna chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Dukaan ka CCTV DVR almari mein locked hai; cashier footage dekh sakta hai par delete nahi kar sakta. Lekin agar cashier poori dukaan (tenant) hi band karwa de aur DVR dukaan ke saath chala jaye -- woh loophole band karna padega.
how_it_works: GRANT SELECT, INSERT only -> UPDATE/DELETE denied. But FK CASCADE from tenants executes as part of permitted DELETE on tenants.
in_this_project: `migrations/versions/0001_initial.py` (grants, `audit_logs ... REFERENCES tenants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE`), `tests/test_rls.py::test_audit_log_is_append_only_for_the_app`, FAILURE_SCENARIOS #6; `migrations/versions/0004_review_hardening.py` (`REVOKE DELETE ON tenants`), `tests/test_review_fixes.py::test_app_role_cannot_delete_tenants`.
disadvantages: CASCADE FK abhi bhi hai -- owner/superuser tenant delete kare toh audit jaata hai (archive pehle karna padega)
common_mistakes: Append-only sirf app code mein enforce karna
Audit table pe CASCADE chhod dena
Audit aur app same credentials pe external copy ke bina
follow_up_questions: Trigger-based audit vs app-level audit?
Hash chain kaise implement karoge?
CDC se audit stream kaise?

question: What happens if a billing webhook is delivered twice, or if someone forges or modifies one?
answer_hinglish:
Duplicate delivery: `verify_and_parse` signature pass karta hai (genuine event), phir `apply_event` `INSERT INTO billing_events (id ...)` pe PK violation -> `IntegrityError` -> return False -> response `{received: true, duplicate: true}` with 200. Plan dobara update nahi hota, audit row dobara nahi banti. Provider ko 200 milta hai toh retry band. Test: `dup.json()['duplicate'] is True`. FAILURE_SCENARIOS #9.

Forged webhook (attacker bina secret ke 'upgrade to enterprise' bhejta hai): woh valid HMAC nahi bana sakta -> 401 'invalid signature'. Modified webhook (genuine captured event mein 'pro' ko 'enterprise' kiya, purana signature rakha): HMAC raw body pe hai, body badli -> mismatch -> 401. Test: `body.replace(b'pro', b'enterprise')` with `prov.sign(body)` (original body ka signature) -> 401. FAILURE_SCENARIOS #10.

Replay of old genuine event after 5 min: timestamp tolerance 300s -> 401. Within 5 min: idempotency -> duplicate, no effect.

Genuine event with unknown plan (provider config galti): `apply_event` `evt.plan not in PLANS` -> 422 Unprocessable -- provider retry karega; yeh theek hai kyunki fix ke baad apply ho jayega.

Out-of-order genuine events (purana 'active' event naye 'canceled' ke baad aaye): review se pehle last write jeet-ta tha; ab `provider_event_at` guard purane event ko record karke ignore karta hai (`test_stale_billing_event_does_not_override_newer_one`). Aur agar secret leak ho jaye toh attacker valid signatures bana sakta hai -- rotation plan chahiye.
why_needed: Payments ke failure modes interview mein specifically poochhe jaate hain -- duplicate, forged, replayed, out-of-order.
real_world_analogy: Cheque: same cheque dobara jama karo toh bank 'already cleared' bolta hai; amount mein ek zero badha do toh signature match nahi karega; 6 mahine purana cheque reject.
how_it_works: Signature check (authenticity+integrity+freshness) -> dedup insert (idempotency) -> plan validation -> apply.
code_example:
# real tests/test_api.py (trimmed)
dup = await c.post("/billing/webhook", content=body, headers={"x-billing-signature": prov.sign(body)})
assert dup.json()["duplicate"] is True
forged = await c.post("/billing/webhook", content=body.replace(b"pro", b"enterprise"),
                      headers={"x-billing-signature": prov.sign(body)})
assert forged.status_code == 401
disadvantages: Ordering relies on provider timestamps; secret leak still means forged-but-valid events
Secret leak = full compromise of billing input
common_mistakes: Signature verify ke pehle JSON parse aur DB lookup
Unknown plan ko silently free bana dena
follow_up_questions: Out-of-order events ke liye provider_event_at guard kaafi hai ya re-fetch bhi chahiye?
Webhook secret rotation?
Provider ka webhook endpoint down rahe 3 din toh?

question: What happens if the worker crashes in the middle of a job?
answer_hinglish:
Job lost ho sakti hai -- is project ka queue at-most-once hai. `process_one` `BRPOP saas:jobs` karta hai: Redis atomically message list se hata ke worker ko deta hai. Ab agar worker crash ho (OOM, deploy, kill -9) handler chalne se pehle ya beech mein: (1) Message Redis se gaya, kahin aur nahi. (2) Handler `tenant_tx` mein tha -- transaction commit nahi hua, toh rollback -- report row 'queued' status mein hi rahegi. (3) Koi retry nahi kyunki koi record nahi ki job in-flight thi. User ko report hamesha 'queued' dikhegi.

Handler exception (crash nahi) ka case handled hai: `except Exception` -> log -> alag `tenant_tx` mein report 'failed' mark. Lekin graceful shutdown bhi handled nahi -- `worker.py` KeyboardInterrupt suppress karta hai, in-flight job ka wait nahi.

Fix options: (a) `BLMOVE saas:jobs saas:jobs:processing` (reliable queue pattern) -- message processing list mein move, success pe LREM, aur reaper jo purane processing items ko wapas queue kare (visibility timeout). (b) Project 3 jaisa proper job queue with leases, retries, backoff, DLQ. (c) DB-backed queue: reports table khud queue hai -- `SELECT ... WHERE status = 'queued' FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` -- aur Redis sirf wake-up signal; crash pe row lock release, doosra worker utha lega. Option (c) yahan natural hai kyunki report row already DB mein hai aur RLS ke saath tenant-scoped.

Aur ek idempotency point: retry aane ke baad handler do baar chal sakta hai -- `project_report` idempotent hai (recompute + UPDATE), toh safe.
why_needed: At-most-once vs at-least-once delivery semantics distributed systems ka core topic hai.
real_world_analogy: Waiter ne order slip board se utha li aur kitchen jaate waqt behosh ho gaya -- slip kahin nahi, customer intezaar karta rahega. Reliable system mein slip 'in progress' tray mein jaati hai.
how_it_works: BRPOP removes message -> crash -> no record -> lost. Reliable: BLMOVE to processing list / SKIP LOCKED on DB rows / leases.
in_this_project: `saas/services/jobs.py::process_one` (BRPOP, except Exception -> mark failed), `saas/worker.py::main`, `saas/api/routes.py::run_report` (row inserted 'queued' before enqueue).
common_mistakes: Stuck 'queued' rows ka monitoring na hona
follow_up_questions: SKIP LOCKED with RLS -- worker ko saare tenants ki rows kaise dikhengi?
Visibility timeout kitna rakhoge?
Exactly-once effect kaise approximate karoge?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: BRPOP simplicity vs reliability; DB-as-queue transactional aur tenant-scoped hai lekin polling/locking DB pe load daalta hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Crash -> lost job; Redis restart without persistence -> poori queue lost; poison message -> har baar fail (abhi mark failed, theek).
advanced.alternatives: Reliable list pattern (BLMOVE + reaper), Redis Streams with consumer groups (XACK, XPENDING), Project 3 queue, Postgres SKIP LOCKED.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 100x jobs pe per-tenant queues + fairness; Streams consumer groups horizontal scale; DB queue pe partial index on status.
advanced.production_improvements: Stuck-job sweeper (queued > N min -> re-enqueue), retries with backoff, DLQ, graceful shutdown (finish current job), queue depth metrics per tenant.

question: What happens to usage data and quotas if Redis loses data, and how would you make metering billing-grade?
answer_hinglish:
Redis loss (restart without persistence, failover to lagging replica, FLUSHDB) ke do effects. (1) Durable record: Postgres `usage_counters` mein last flush tak ka value hai (worker har 60s). Last flush ke baad ke counts lost -- README: 'a Redis loss loses unflushed counts.' Agle flush pe GREATEST ki wajah se chhota Redis value Postgres ko overwrite nahi karega -- DB value peeche nahi jaayegi, lekin aage bhi nahi badhegi jab tak Redis counter purane DB value ko cross na kare. Matlab us mahine ke liye undercounting: Redis 0 se count karega, DB pe 8,000 tha; Redis 5,000 pe pahunche tab bhi DB 8,000 dikhayega -- 5,000 naye calls billing mein gayab. (2) Quota enforcement: `meter` sirf Redis value pe compare karta hai, toh Redis reset = quota reset -- tenant mahine mein dobara poora quota use kar sakta hai.

TRADEOFFS #8 yeh consciously accept karta hai -- quota enforcement 'soft' hai. Billing-grade ke liye: (a) Redis restart pe counter ko DB value se seed karo -- `SET key db_value NX` pehle INCR se (ya Lua: if not exists, set from arg). (b) Flush ko delta-based banao with idempotency: Redis mein `INCR` ke saath `flushed` marker; ya events-based. (c) Best: har billable event ko durable log (Kafka) mein likho, aggregation downstream (ClickHouse/warehouse), aur invoice usi se -- counters sirf enforcement ke liye. (d) Redis persistence AOF everysec, replicas with WAIT. Accuracy vs cost: per-request durable write mehenga hai, isliye event batching.
why_needed: Usage-based billing mein undercounting = revenue loss, overcounting = customer trust loss; dono ka reasoning chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Dukaan ka din ka cash counter reset ho gaya: register mein subah ka total likha hai, lekin dopahar ki bikri ka hisaab gaya; aur agar register 'jo bada ho wahi likho' rule follow kare toh shaam tak naya count register se chhota rahega aur update hi nahi hoga.
how_it_works: Redis counter reset -> quota reset; flush GREATEST keeps old DB value -> undercount until Redis exceeds it.
code_example:
# illustrative seed-on-miss (not in repo)
SEED_INCR = """
if redis.call('EXISTS', KEYS[1]) == 0 then redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[1], 'EX', ARGV[2]) end
return redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
"""
# ARGV[1] = value from usage_counters (cached per tenant/period)
common_mistakes: Counters ko billing source of truth banana
Redis without persistence for billing data
follow_up_questions: Seed-on-miss ka race kaise handle?
Event log vs counters billing ke liye?
Customer usage dispute kaise resolve karoge?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Counters cheap aur fast; events accurate aur auditable par storage aur pipeline cost. Enforcement aur billing ko alag systems banana common pattern hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Redis failover to stale replica -> partial loss; worker down long time -> big loss window; clock/month boundary -> counts in wrong period.
advanced.alternatives: Kafka usage events -> stream aggregation; Postgres append-only usage_events with periodic rollup; provider-side metered billing (Stripe usage records) with idempotency keys.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 100x tenants pe flush SCAN + per-key tx impractical -> batch upsert ya streaming; per-tenant usage sharded counters.
advanced.production_improvements: Seed-on-miss, AOF, flush lag alert, reconciliation job (events vs counters), invoice from event store.

question: Tell me about the cross-tenant privilege escalation bug: symptom, investigation, root cause, fix.
answer_hinglish:
Yeh meri sabse achhi debugging story hai. Symptom: `test_tenant_isolation_over_http` fail hua. Bob (sirf Globex ka owner) `/t/acme/projects` pe 404 expect tha, 200 mila. Matlab Bob Acme ka data dekh pa raha tha.

Investigation: (1) Pehle dekha kaun si layer allow kar rahi hai -- 200 ka matlab `tenant_principal` ko role mila. (2) `/t/acme` (tenant_info) call kiya Bob ke token se -- role 'owner' aaya! Bob Acme ka owner treat ho raha tha -- sirf read leak nahi, full escalation. (3) Role lookup query dekhi: `SELECT role FROM memberships WHERE user_id = :u` -- tenant filter nahi, kyunki 'RLS scope kar dega'. (4) Memberships policy dekhi: `USING (tenant_id = app.tenant_id OR user_id = app.user_id)`. OR clause 'my workspaces' list ke liye add kiya tha. Ab Acme context mein Bob ki Globex membership row OR ke second part se visible thi, aur query ne wahi row ('owner') return kar di.

Root cause: do individually reasonable decisions -- permissive policy aur RLS pe rely karne wali query -- milke invariant todte hain. Invariant tha 'tenant context mein unfiltered query sirf us tenant ki rows dekhti hai'; OR ne usse silently tod diya.

Fix (migration 0003 + code): (a) memberships policy strict -- sirf tenant_id, no OR. (b) 'My workspaces' ke liye `user_tenants(p_user)` SECURITY DEFINER function; `my_tenants` usse use karta hai. (c) Membership role queries mein explicit `WHERE tenant_id = :t AND user_id = :u` (deps, change_role, remove_member). (d) SQL-level regression test `test_unfiltered_membership_query_cannot_return_other_tenant_roles`. Lesson: policy mein OR = escape hatch; cross-tenant needs ko named, narrow functions mein daalo.
why_needed: Real bug story with clear root cause aur layered fix -- interviewers yahi sunna pasand karte hain. Yeh flagship story hai.
real_world_analogy: Society ka rule 'resident apne flat ki chaabi le sakta hai, YA apne naam ki koi bhi chaabi' -- Bob ne Acme building mein 'apne naam ki chaabi' maangi aur Globex ki master chaabi mil gayi, jo Acme ke lock pe bhi chal gayi kyunki guard ne sirf naam dekha.
how_it_works: OR policy -> row from tenant B visible in tenant A context -> user-only filter picks it -> role 'owner' -> Principal with owner perms in A.
in_this_project: `migrations/versions/0003_strict_memberships_policy.py` (docstring explains the bug; downgrade shows the old OR policy), `saas/api/deps.py::tenant_principal` (explicit filter comment), `saas/services/tenancy.py::my_tenants`, tests `test_tenant_isolation_over_http`, `test_unfiltered_membership_query_cannot_return_other_tenant_roles`, TESTING.md bug #1.
code_example:
-- before (0001, now reverted by 0003)
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON memberships
  USING (tenant_id = nullif(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid
         OR user_id = nullif(current_setting('app.user_id', true), '')::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = nullif(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid);
-- buggy lookup inside tenant A's context:
SELECT role FROM memberships WHERE user_id = :bob;   -- returned Bob's 'owner' row from Globex
advantages: Caught by an HTTP isolation test before shipping
Fix at policy level + code level + regression test
disadvantages: Bug existed because both layers trusted each other
Required a new SECURITY DEFINER function (new surface)
common_mistakes: Policy mein OR convenience ke liye
RLS pe rely karke sensitive lookups mein tenant filter chhodna
Sirf app-level fix karna aur policy loose chhod dena
follow_up_questions: Yeh bug production mein hota toh kaise detect karte?
Permissive vs restrictive policies (AS RESTRICTIVE) se kya madad milti?
Aise bugs ke liye kaunse tests standard banaoge?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Strict policies + explicit definer functions = thoda zyada code par invariant simple; permissive OR = convenience par har query ko reason karna padega.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar test na hota: koi bhi user jo kisi tenant ka owner hai, kisi bhi tenant ka owner ban jaata (sirf slug chahiye) -- full cross-tenant takeover.
advanced.alternatives: Restrictive policy layering (AS RESTRICTIVE tenant check + permissive user check) jo AND semantics deti; separate view for 'my memberships'; app-only lookups with mandatory tenant filter.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Bade codebase mein policies ka review process aur policy tests auto-generated per table (har table pe 'other tenant row invisible even with user filter').
advanced.production_improvements: Policy linting in CI (no OR in tenant policies), cross-tenant HTTP tests for every new route, runtime assertion Principal.tenant_id == membership row tenant_id, audit alert on role resolved != expected tenant.

question: A query unexpectedly returns zero rows in production. How do you debug an RLS issue?
answer_hinglish:
RLS ka sabse common symptom 'zero rows' hai -- aur yeh fail-closed design ka by-product hai. Step by step: (1) Same transaction mein context check: `SELECT current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), current_setting('app.user_id', true), current_user`. Agar NULL/'' hai toh code `global_tx` mein hai ya context set hone se pehle query chal gayi, ya transaction ke bahar (autocommit) set_config hua aur turant khatam. (2) Role check: `current_user` saas_app hai? Agar owner/superuser hota toh zyada rows aati, kam nahi -- toh yeh opposite symptom. (3) Policy check: `SELECT * FROM pg_policies WHERE tablename = 'projects'` -- policy expression kya hai, permissive/restrictive. (4) Data check owner role se (RLS bypass): `SELECT tenant_id, count(*) FROM projects GROUP BY 1` -- kya rows sach mein us tenant_id ke saath hain? Galat tenant_id se insert hua ho sakta hai (lekin WITH CHECK yeh rokta hai). (5) Type issue: tenant id string format -- `nullif(...)::uuid` cast; invalid string pe error aata, zero rows nahi. (6) Cache: kya yeh response cache se aaya (`projects:list` stale empty list)? Redis key check karo `saas:cache:{tenant}:projects:list`. (7) SECURITY DEFINER flows: API key lookup global context mein `SELECT FROM api_keys` 0 deta hai -- function use karo.

Project-specific: tests mein `test_context_does_not_leak_between_transactions` dikhata hai ki naye transaction mein setting `None` ya `''` hoti hai -- isliye agar koi code `async with sm() as s` seedha use kare `tenant_tx` ke bina, woh zero rows dekhega. TRADEOFFS #2 is debugging surprise ko cost ke roop mein list karta hai.
why_needed: RLS ke saath kaam karne wala har engineer yeh debug karta hai; structured approach dikhana zaroori.
real_world_analogy: Fridge khaali dikh raha hai: pehle dekho tumne apna naam ka badge lagaya (context), sahi fridge hai (role), rule kya hai (policy), aur khaana sach mein tumhare shelf pe rakha tha (data).
how_it_works: Check context -> role -> policies (pg_policies) -> data as owner -> cache -> code path (tenant_tx vs raw session).
disadvantages: Owner access debugging ke liye chahiye (sensitive)
common_mistakes: Owner role se reproduce karke 'mere pe toh chal raha' kehna
follow_up_questions: Development mein context missing pe error kaise raise karoge?
pg_policies ka qual column kya dikhata hai?
Production pe owner access kaun le sakta hai?

question: Describe the asyncpg 'one type per bind parameter' bug and how you fixed it.
answer_hinglish:
Symptom: tenant creation ke audit insert pe error aaya. Original query kuch aisi thi: `INSERT INTO audit_logs (tenant_id, actor_user_id, action, target_type, target_id) VALUES (:t, :u, 'tenant.created', 'tenant', :t)` -- tenant id do baar, ek baar `tenant_id` (uuid column) mein aur ek baar `target_id` (text column) mein, same `:t` parameter.

Root cause: asyncpg extended protocol use karta hai. Statement prepare hota hai aur Postgres har placeholder (`$1`, `$2`) ka EK type infer karta hai. SQLAlchemy `:t` ko ek hi `$1` mein convert karta hai. Ab `$1` ek jagah uuid context mein hai aur doosri jagah text context mein -- Postgres ek type choose karta hai (jaise uuid), aur doosre usage pe type mismatch error ('column target_id is of type text but expression is of type uuid' ya inconsistent types deduced). psycopg (client-side interpolation) mein yeh chal jaata kyunki value literal ban jaati hai -- isliye yeh driver-specific surprise hai.

Fix: alag parameter -- `:tt` for target_id with `str(tid)`. `create_tenant` mein comment: 'Separate :tt param: asyncpg infers ONE type per parameter, and target_id is text, tenant_id uuid.' Same pattern `accept_invitation` mein `:ut` aur `audit.record` mein `:ti` (str(target_id)). Alternative: explicit CAST `CAST(:t AS text)`. TESTING.md bug #2.

Debugging tip: aise errors mein Postgres error message mein parameter number aur deduced type hota hai; `log_statement` ya asyncpg debug se actual prepared SQL dekho.
why_needed: Driver-level gotchas production debugging ka hissa hain; yeh dikhata hai ki aap ORM ke neeche kya ho raha hai samajhte ho.
real_world_analogy: Form mein ek hi khana 'ID' do jagah use kiya -- ek jagah number chahiye, ek jagah naam; form wala ek baar decide karta hai ki khana number ka hai, doosri jagah reject.
how_it_works: Named param :t -> single $1 -> server-side type inference picks one type -> conflicting contexts fail. Fix: distinct params or explicit casts.
code_example:
# real services/tenancy.py
# Separate :tt param: asyncpg infers ONE type per parameter, and target_id is text, tenant_id uuid.
await s.execute(text("INSERT INTO audit_logs (tenant_id, actor_user_id, action, target_type, target_id) "
                     "VALUES (:t, :u, 'tenant.created', 'tenant', :tt)"), {"t": tid, "u": user_id, "tt": str(tid)})
common_mistakes: Same param ko different-typed columns mein reuse
psycopg pe test, asyncpg pe deploy

question: A migration fails with 'cannot insert multiple commands into a prepared statement'. What is going on?
answer_hinglish:
Yeh error asyncpg + multi-statement SQL ka classic hai -- TESTING.md bug #3: 'Migration with multiple statements per execute failed under asyncpg's extended protocol: split.'

Investigation: (1) Error message hi hint hai -- 'prepared statement' matlab extended protocol. (2) `migrations/env.py` dekha: `create_async_engine(_url())` -- asyncpg driver. (3) Migration `op.execute(big_sql_string)` jisme `CREATE EXTENSION ...; CREATE TABLE users ...; CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ...;` ek saath.

Cause: Postgres wire protocol ke do modes. Simple Query ('Q' message) ek string mein multiple `;`-separated statements allow karta hai. Extended Query (Parse/Bind/Execute) ek Parse mein ek statement. asyncpg `execute()` with no args simple protocol use kar sakta hai, lekin SQLAlchemy ke through jaane pe prepared path hota hai -- multi-statement reject.

Fix: `run(sql)` helper -- `';\n'` pe split, comment-only chunks skip, har statement alag `op.execute`. Constraint: statement bodies (plpgsql `DO $$...$$`, function bodies) mein `;\n` nahi hona chahiye -- isliye role-creation `DO` block aur 0002/0003 functions separate `op.execute` calls hain. Alternative fixes: migrations sync driver (psycopg) se chalana, ya raw asyncpg connection `conn.execute(script)` (simple protocol) via `op.get_bind()`.

Verification: fresh DB pe `alembic -x url=... upgrade head` aur phir test suite -- tests real schema pe chalte hain.
why_needed: Tooling/driver debugging -- real-world aur interview dono mein useful.
real_world_analogy: ATM ek baar mein ek hi transaction leta hai; tum 'withdraw 500; balance check; withdraw 200' ek slip pe likh doge toh reject. Teen slips banao.
how_it_works: Extended protocol: one statement per Parse. Split script -> N executes. Bodies with ';\n' need whole execution.
in_this_project: `migrations/versions/0001_initial.py::run`, `migrations/env.py` (async engine), TESTING.md bug #3, TESTING.md command `alembic -x url=... upgrade head`.
code_example:
-- illustrative failing call
-- op.execute("CREATE TABLE a (id int); CREATE TABLE b (id int);")
-- asyncpg: cannot insert multiple commands into a prepared statement
advantages: Root cause understood at protocol level
disadvantages: Split helper fragile for complex bodies
common_mistakes: Split helper ko function bodies pe use karna
follow_up_questions: Migrations ke liye sync vs async driver?
Transactional DDL Postgres mein kya guarantee deta hai?
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY migrations mein kaise chalaoge?

question: A customer says a removed member could still access the tenant for a short time. How do you investigate?
answer_hinglish:
Pehle expected behaviour samjho: removal ke baad access kaise rukta hai. Access token (JWT) 15 min valid rehta hai -- revocation nahi. Lekin har tenant request pe membership role check hota hai (`tenant_principal` -> cache `member-role:{user_id}` -> DB), aur `DELETE /members/{id}` commit ke baad cache key invalidate karta hai. Toh expected: agli request se 404.

Access kab reh sakta hai: (1) Cache invalidation fail -- Redis error swallow hota hai (`invalidate` mein `except RedisError: pass`); stale role TTL (60s) tak. (2) Stale-set race -- removal se pehle shuru hui request ne old role DB se padha aur invalidate ke baad cache mein SET kiya; 60s tak. (3) API key -- agar removed user ne key banayi thi, key ka creator role lookup DB se direct hai (cache nahi), toh role None -> empty perms -> sab 403. Lekin key khud revoke nahi hoti, aur perm-less key se requests abhi bhi `tenant_principal` pass karti hain (metered, rate limited) -- data nahi milta. (4) Platform-level routes (`/me`) access token se chalte hain -- removed member `/me` pe us tenant ko nahi dekhega kyunki `user_tenants()` DB se live hai.

Investigation: audit log mein `member.removed` timestamp aur `request_id`; access logs (bpcommon JSON logs with request id, path, status) mein removed user ke requests after that timestamp; dekho kis time tak 200 aaye -- agar <= 60s toh cache path. Redis error metrics us waqt. Fix: removal ke liye cache bypass/deny-key, versioned keys, aur invalidation failures pe alert.
why_needed: Production incident handling: expected behaviour, possible windows, evidence-based investigation.
real_world_analogy: Employee ko nikala, HR ne system mein entry kar di, lekin gate ke guard ke paas subah ki printed list hai -- agli list (TTL) aane tak andar aa sakta hai.
how_it_works: Removal commit -> DEL member-role key. Windows: invalidate failure, stale-set race (<= TTL), JWT validity irrelevant for tenant routes.
advantages: Audit + request ids allow precise timeline
common_mistakes: JWT ko blame karna bina check kiye (tenant routes per-request membership check karte hain)
Logs mein request id na hona
Cache TTL ko security-critical data ke liye lamba rakhna
follow_up_questions: Window ko zero kaise karoge bina cache hataye?
Removed member ki API keys ka kya karna chahiye?
Customer ko kya batayoge (SLA)?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Caching role lookups latency bachata hai; security events ke liye strong consistency chahiye -- hybrid: cache with version/deny keys.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Redis partition during removal -> stale for TTL; multi-region caches -> longer windows.
advanced.alternatives: No role caching (indexed PK lookup ~sub-ms on DB); pub/sub invalidation; short TTL (5s) for roles.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Bade tenants mein frequent membership churn -- versioned per-tenant membership epoch in tenant row (already cached) so one bump invalidates all roles.
advanced.production_improvements: Invalidation failure metric + retry, deny-key on removal, auto-revoke keys created by removed members, incident runbook with log queries by request_id.

question: A tenant reports frequent 429 errors. How do you figure out whether it is the rate limit or the quota?
answer_hinglish:
Error body pehla clue hai: rate limit -> `{"error": {"code": "rate_limited", "details": {"plan": ...}}}` with `Retry-After` header; quota -> `code: "quota_exceeded"` with `details: {used, limit}`, aur Retry-After nahi. Customer se response body ya request_id maango; ya hamare JSON access logs mein us tenant ke 429s dekho (bpcommon middleware har request status log karta hai, Prometheus `http_requests_total{status="429"}` route ke saath).

Rate limit case: `saas:rl:{tenant_id}` hash dekho -- `HGETALL` se tokens aur ts. Plan ke `requests_per_second` aur `burst` compare karo (free 5/10, pro 50/100). Tenant ke saare users aur API keys ek hi bucket share karte hain -- toh ek CI job ya integration jo burst bhejti hai woh poore tenant ke UI users ko 429 dila sakti hai. Fix options: customer ko client-side backoff with Retry-After, upgrade, ya per-key/per-user sub-limits.

Quota case: `GET /t/{slug}/usage` (period, api_calls, monthly_quota) ya Redis `saas:usage:{tid}:api_calls:{YYYY-MM}`. Note: har request meter hoti hai jo `tenant_principal` pass kare -- 403 permission failures bhi count hoti hain (metering route ke permission check se pehle). Toh buggy client jo baar baar 403 le raha hai woh bhi quota kha raha hai. Aur rate-limited requests meter nahi hoti (check_rate pehle raise karta hai). Platform admin `/admin/tenants/{id}/usage` historical months dikhata hai.

Test reference: `test_tenant_rate_limit_and_quota` dono paths dikhata hai -- 15 rapid calls mein 429 rate_limited, phir usage key 10,000 set karke quota_exceeded.
why_needed: Support/debugging scenario jo real SaaS mein roz aata hai; distinct error codes ka value yahan dikhta hai.
real_world_analogy: Mobile pe 'network busy, thodi der baad try karo' (rate) vs 'data pack khatam' (quota) -- message padh ke hi pata chal jaata hai kaunsa problem hai.
how_it_works: 429 body code -> rate_limited: inspect bucket + plan rps/burst; quota_exceeded: inspect usage counter + plan monthly quota.
in_this_project: `saas/services/limits.py::TenantLimits` (`check_rate` with Retry-After, `meter` with QuotaExceeded details), `saas/api/routes.py::usage`, `shared/bpcommon/http.py` (metrics/logs), test `test_tenant_rate_limit_and_quota`.
code_example:
# illustrative redis-cli checks
# HGETALL saas:rl:<tenant_id>
# GET saas:usage:<tenant_id>:api_calls:2026-11
disadvantages: Shared tenant bucket -- one client starves others
common_mistakes: Quota ko rate limit samajh ke Retry-After pe retry loop
follow_up_questions: Per-API-key limits kaise add karoge?
Kya 4xx responses ko meter karna chahiye?
Quota warning (80%) notification kaise?

question: Defend the choice of pooled tenancy with RLS over schema-per-tenant or database-per-tenant.
answer_hinglish:
Main is project ke target ke hisaab se defend karta hoon: bahut saare chhote-medium B2B tenants, ek chhoti team. Pooled ke fayde: ek schema, ek migration (0001-0003 ek baar chalti hain, N baar nahi); connection pooling simple (ek DB, ek pool -- DB-per-tenant mein N pools ya routing); cheapest per tenant (free tier economically possible); cross-tenant analytics aur platform admin queries simple; tenant onboarding ek INSERT hai, DB provisioning nahi. Industry mein most B2B SaaS isi se start karte hain.

Kamzori aur meri mitigation: (1) Isolation logical hai -- ek bug leak kar sakta hai. Mitigation: RLS ENABLE + FORCE, non-owner NOBYPASSRLS app role, fail-closed context, SQL-level tests, aur defence-in-depth explicit filters. (2) Noisy neighbour -- plan-based per-tenant rate limits, tenant-first indexes; aage per-tenant timeouts aur silos. (3) Per-tenant restore mushkil -- documented gap (SYSTEM_DESIGN.md), PITR + filtered extract. (4) Postgres bug ya SECURITY DEFINER mistake -- TRADEOFFS #1 honestly kehta hai yeh leak kar sakta hai.

Schema-per-tenant kyun nahi: hazaron schemas pe catalog bloat, migrations N baar (aur partial failure), pg_dump slow, connection search_path management -- aur isolation phir bhi same DB process mein. DB-per-tenant kyun nahi: cost aur ops 10-100x, free tier impossible. Kab badlunga: regulated customer physical isolation maange, ya ek tenant ka load doosron ko hurt kare -- tab hybrid: us tenant ko silo, baaki pool.
why_needed: Senior interviewers aapke core architectural choice ko challenge karte hain; balanced defence with mitigations aur exit criteria chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Co-working space vs har startup ka alag office: shuruat mein co-working (sasta, shared reception) with achhe locks; jab koi company bahut badi ya sensitive ho jaaye, usse private floor.
how_it_works: Pooled + RLS = shared everything with DB-enforced row isolation; exit path = per-tenant silo via routing.
in_this_project: TRADEOFFS.md #1, #2; SYSTEM_DESIGN.md isolation table; ARCHITECTURE.md 'Tenancy model choice'; migrations 0001/0003; tests/test_rls.py.
common_mistakes: Pooled chunna bina RLS ya equivalent backstop
follow_up_questions: Compliance auditor ko pooled isolation kaise prove karoge?
Data residency (EU) requirement aaye toh?
Kitne tenants pe schema-per-tenant toot-ta hai?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Cost/ops vs isolation strength; pooled + RLS beech ka point hai -- strong logical isolation, cheap. Hybrid future-proofing deta hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: RLS bypass via misconfig (owner role), definer bug, Postgres CVE -> potential cross-tenant leak; whale tenant -> shared degradation.
advanced.alternatives: Schema-per-tenant (tens-hundreds tenants), DB-per-tenant (regulated/large), Citus distributed pooled, cell architecture.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x: pooled still fine with PgBouncer/replicas. 100x: partitioning/Citus + silos for top tier.
advanced.production_improvements: Compliance evidence: RLS tests in CI, role audits, pen tests; tenant move tooling; per-tenant encryption keys for stronger logical isolation.

question: Why use RLS as a backstop instead of relying only on application-level tenant filtering?
answer_hinglish:
Application-only filtering ka matlab: har query mein developer ko `WHERE tenant_id = :t` yaad rakhna hai -- har nayi query, har refactor, har background job, har admin script, har junior developer. Ek miss = data breach, aur code review mein yeh miss hona aasaan hai kyunki 'missing code' dikhta nahi. Probability chhoti lekin cost existential.

RLS database level pe invariant deta hai: 'tenant context mein koi bhi query sirf us tenant ki rows dekhegi'. `test_unfiltered_query_sees_only_current_tenant` aur `test_tenant_aware_background_job` (handler mein jaan boojh kar filter nahi) prove karte hain. TRADEOFFS #2: 'RLS catches forgotten WHERE clauses (proven)'.

RLS ke costs (honest): (1) per-transaction `set_config` -- ek extra statement/round trip. (2) SECURITY DEFINER functions cross-tenant needs ke liye -- naya attack surface aur review burden. (3) Debugging surprises -- 'zero rows kyun?'. (4) Performance -- generally negligible (benchmark mein policy Index Cond bani), lekin complex policies (subqueries, functions) slow ho sakti hain. (5) Operational care -- app role ka setup sahi hona chahiye warna RLS silently off.

Maine dono rakhe -- 'backstop' word important hai. App layer primary authorization hai (membership, permissions, ABAC), aur sensitive queries mein explicit filters bhi; RLS woh net hai jo galti ko breach banne se rokta hai. Escalation bug ne dikhaya ki layers ek doosre ko cover karti hain -- aur jab dono weak hon tab kya hota hai.
why_needed: Yeh 'why RLS' ka core justification hai; costs ke saath balanced answer chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Car mein achha driver (app filters) bhi chahiye aur seatbelt (RLS) bhi; seatbelt ki wajah se rash driving nahi karte, lekin galti pe jaan bachti hai.
how_it_works: App filters: explicit, visible, developer-dependent. RLS: implicit, enforced, role/config-dependent. Together: defence in depth.
in_this_project: TRADEOFFS.md #2; `saas/services/jobs.py::project_report` (no filter by design); `saas/api/deps.py` explicit filter on role lookup; tests in `tests/test_rls.py`.
common_mistakes: RLS hai toh app checks hata dena
RLS ko owner role ke saath 'test' karna
follow_up_questions: RLS ke bina ORM-level automatic scoping kitna safe hai?
Policy mein subquery (memberships join) kab theek hai?
RLS migrations mein policies ka versioning?

question: Why did you decide 'no OR in RLS policies'? What does it cost?
answer_hinglish:
Rule: tenant table ki policy ek hi condition rakhegi -- `tenant_id = current tenant`. Koi 'OR user apni rows dekh sakta hai', 'OR admin', 'OR public flag' nahi. Kyun? Kyunki RLS ka value ek simple invariant mein hai: 'tenant context mein unfiltered query bhi sirf us tenant ki rows deti hai'. Har developer is invariant pe rely karke code likhta hai (jaise `SELECT role FROM memberships WHERE user_id = :u`). OR clause is invariant ko silently todta hai -- ab har query ko reason karna padega ki kya OR ki rows bhi aa sakti hain. Mere project mein exactly yahi hua: memberships pe `OR user_id = app.user_id` ne Bob ko Acme ka owner bana diya (migration 0003 docstring: 'An OR in a policy breaks the invariant "an unfiltered query is still tenant-safe"').

Cross-tenant needs kaise poore hote hain: named, narrow SECURITY DEFINER functions -- `user_tenants(p_user)` ('my workspaces'), `resolve_api_key(p_hash)`, `accept_invitation_lookup(p_hash)`. Har ek ek specific question ka answer deta hai, minimal columns ke saath, aur code mein explicitly dikhta hai ki 'yahan cross-tenant read ho raha hai'.

Cost: (1) zyada code -- har cross-tenant use case ke liye function + migration + grant. (2) Har definer function ek RLS bypass hai jise review karna padta hai. (3) Policies alone se 'user ke saare memberships' query nahi likh sakte. TRADEOFFS #4: 'slightly more code, but the invariant holds'. Postgres alternative: permissive + `AS RESTRICTIVE` policies combine karna (restrictive policies AND hoti hain) -- tenant check restrictive rakho toh OR wali permissive policy tenant boundary nahi tod sakti.
why_needed: Policy design principle aur real bug se nikla lesson -- senior-level reasoning.
real_world_analogy: Ghar ke main door pe ek hi rule: 'sirf ghar ki chaabi'. 'Ya phir koi bhi jiske paas kisi bhi ghar ki chaabi ho' jod diya toh poori colony ki chaabiyan kaam karne lagengi.
how_it_works: Single-predicate policies keep invariant; exceptions as explicit functions; or RESTRICTIVE tenant policy ANDed with permissive ones.
in_this_project: `migrations/versions/0003_strict_memberships_policy.py` (docstring + strict policy + user_tenants), TRADEOFFS.md #4, DATABASE_DESIGN.md ('Policies contain no OR escape hatches').
code_example:
-- illustrative RESTRICTIVE alternative (not in repo)
CREATE POLICY tenant_guard ON memberships AS RESTRICTIVE
  USING (tenant_id = nullif(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid);
-- any PERMISSIVE policy added later is ANDed with tenant_guard, so it can't cross tenants
advantages: Prevents the bug class, not just the bug
disadvantages: Each function is a privileged surface
common_mistakes: Policy changes without cross-tenant regression tests
follow_up_questions: RESTRICTIVE vs PERMISSIVE policies ka exact semantics?
Agar 'public projects' feature chahiye toh?
Policies ko CI mein lint kaise karoge?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Strictness vs convenience; restrictive policies ek beech ka raasta hai jo policy level pe flexibility deta hai bina tenant boundary tode.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Future developer 'chhota sa OR' add kare -> same bug class wapas; definer function bug -> leak.
advanced.alternatives: AS RESTRICTIVE tenant policy; separate views per access pattern; app-only cross-tenant service with its own BYPASSRLS role.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Features badhenge (sharing across tenants, marketplace) -- explicit sharing tables (grants) with their own policies, not ORs.
advanced.production_improvements: CI check on pg_policies (no OR in qual for tenant tables), auto-generated cross-tenant tests per table, mandatory security review for new definer functions.

question: Stateless JWT access tokens versus server-side sessions: what did you trade?
answer_hinglish:
Server-side session: login pe random session id cookie mein, aur har request pe sessions table/Redis lookup. Fayda: instant revocation (row delete karo), session data server pe. Nuksaan: har request pe ek store hit, store scale aur availability ki zimmedari.

Stateless JWT: token khud signed claims carry karta hai; verify CPU-only (HMAC). Fayda: koi per-request lookup nahi, horizontal scaling trivial, services token independently verify kar sakti hain. Nuksaan: expiry se pehle revoke nahi ho sakta, aur token mein jo data hai woh stale ho sakta hai.

Mera hybrid: access token stateless JWT 15 min (`access_token_ttl_seconds=900`) -- sirf `sub`, `typ`, `exp`, `iat`, `jti`. Role/permissions JWT mein NAHI hain -- kyunki role tenant-specific hai aur badal sakta hai; har tenant request membership DB/cache se check karti hai. Refresh token stateful hai -- DB mein hashed, rotate, revocable. Toh 'stateful' part sirf har 15 min ek baar hit hota hai.

TRADEOFFS #5: 'No DB hit per request for auth; logout/permission changes take up to 15 minutes to affect access tokens (membership/role is still checked per request, which narrows that window to tenant-level changes only).' Matlab: tenant se nikala gaya user turant bahar (membership check); lekin logout ke baad bhi access token user-level routes (`/me`, `/tenants`) pe 15 min chalega.
why_needed: Classic auth trade-off; har backend interview mein.
real_world_analogy: Movie ticket (JWT) vs club membership card jo har baar reception pe swipe hota hai (session). Ticket fast hai par cancel nahi hota; card har baar check hota hai par cancel turant.
how_it_works: Access: JWT verify (CPU). Refresh: DB lookup + rotation every <= 15 min. Authorization: per-request membership.
disadvantages: Logout not immediate for access token
common_mistakes: Refresh token bhi stateless JWT banana (revocation gone)
follow_up_questions: jti denylist ka cost aur design?
Cookie vs Authorization header?
Microservices mein JWT verify kaise share karoge?

question: Rate limits and quotas fail open when Redis is unavailable. Defend or criticise that choice.
answer_hinglish:
Defend: rate limiter ka purpose abuse aur noisy-neighbour protection hai, core business function nahi. Redis outage ya blip pe fail-closed ka matlab: saare tenants, including paying enterprise customers, ko 429/503 -- poora product down sirf isliye ki ek supporting component down hai. Availability usually zyada valuable hai. TRADEOFFS #9: 'Paying customers keep working through a Redis blip; abuse protection is temporarily off (monitor it).' Quota bhi same (#8). Cache bhi fail open (optimisation hai).

Criticise: (1) Abuse window -- attacker Redis ko overload karke (ya outage ke dauraan) unlimited requests bhej sakta hai; downstream Postgres pe unprotected load aa sakta hai -- jo khud outage cause kar sakta hai (cascading failure). (2) Silent -- code mein RedisError pe sirf return hai, koi log ya metric nahi. Ops ko pata hi nahi chalega ki limits off hain. (3) Quota undercount = revenue loss.

Mera balanced view: fail open theek hai, lekin teen conditions ke saath: (a) loud -- metric/alert on every fail-open (abhi missing, code observation); (b) bounded -- local in-process fallback limiter (per-replica coarse token bucket) taaki complete unlimited na ho; (c) context-specific -- login/registration aur expensive endpoints (reports, exports) ke liye fail closed better ho sakta hai. Edge layer (gateway/WAF) pe independent IP-based limits bhi rakho (DEPLOYMENT.md item 5) -- toh Redis-based tenant limit ek hi defense nahi.
why_needed: Fail-open vs fail-closed trade-off security aur reliability ke beech ka classic dilemma hai.
real_world_analogy: Traffic signal kharab ho gaya: sab gaadiyan rok do (fail closed -- jam) ya chalne do (fail open -- risk). Achha jawab: chalne do, lekin traffic police (fallback) khada karo aur control room ko alert.
how_it_works: RedisError -> return (allow). Missing: metric, local fallback, per-endpoint policy.
code_example:
# illustrative: loud fail-open with local fallback (not in repo)
except RedisError:
    LIMITER_FAIL_OPEN.labels("rate").inc()          # Prometheus counter -> alert
    if not local_bucket.allow(tenant_id, plan):      # coarse per-replica fallback
        raise TooManyRequests("tenant rate limit exceeded (degraded)")
    return
common_mistakes: Har endpoint ke liye same policy
Sirf ek layer of rate limiting
follow_up_questions: Kaunse endpoints fail closed hone chahiye?
Local fallback limiter ka sizing per replica?
Circuit breaker Redis calls ke liye?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Availability vs protection; per-endpoint policy best -- business endpoints open, security endpoints closed.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Redis down + traffic spike -> Postgres overload -> full outage (fail-open backfires); attackers induce Redis slowness.
advanced.alternatives: Gateway/edge rate limiting independent of Redis; local token buckets with periodic sync; circuit breaker that short-circuits Redis calls.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Bigger scale pe Redis Cluster HA aur multi-AZ; limits at multiple layers (CDN, gateway, app).
advanced.production_improvements: Fail-open metrics + alerts, local fallback, Redis call timeouts tight (abhi pool timeout 2s), runbook.

question: Why are plans defined in code rather than in a database table?
answer_hinglish:
`core/plans.py` mein `PLANS` dict hai with frozen `Plan` dataclasses. Docstring: 'Code, not DB rows: plan changes are deploys reviewed like code; per-tenant overrides would go in a table.'

Fayde: (1) Review -- plan limit badalna (free 3 se 5 projects) PR se guzarta hai, history git mein, aur tests usse cover karte hain (`test_plan_entitlements_...` free ke 3 projects pe depend karta hai). (2) Type safety -- dataclass fields, frozen (runtime mein accidental mutation nahi). (3) Zero lookup -- `get_plan(name)` dict lookup, koi DB/cache call nahi hot path pe. (4) Consistency -- saari replicas same deploy pe same plans. (5) Simple -- plans rarely badalte hain.

Nuksaan: (1) Sales ko custom deal chahiye ('Acme ko 75 projects at pro price') -- code mein per-tenant cheez nahi daal sakte; overrides table chahiye (TRADEOFFS #7). (2) Plan change = deploy. (3) Grandfathering -- purane customers ko purane limits pe rakhna (plan versioning: 'pro_2025', 'pro_2026'). (4) `get_plan` unknown name pe free return karta hai -- typo ya DB mein purana plan naam silently free ban jayega (safe default -- downgrade, not upgrade -- lekin silent).

Billing side `apply_event` `evt.plan not in PLANS` pe 422 deta hai, aur `CheckoutIn` pattern `^(free|pro|enterprise)$` -- toh provider se aaye plan names code ke saath validated hain.
why_needed: Configuration-as-code vs data-driven config ka trade-off common design question hai.
real_world_analogy: Restaurant ka printed menu (code) -- badalne ke liye naya print (deploy), lekin sab tables pe same; VIP ke liye 'chef special' ek alag register (overrides table).
how_it_works: PLANS dict -> get_plan(tenant.plan) -> Principal.plan. Overrides would merge: effective = base plan + tenant overrides.
common_mistakes: Plans DB mein bina caching (hot path lookup)
Custom deals ke liye code mein if tenant == 'acme'
follow_up_questions: Overrides table ka design?
Grandfathering kaise?
Unknown plan pe free vs error?

question: Metering in Redis with periodic flush versus writing usage directly to Postgres or a stream: how did you decide?
answer_hinglish:
Teen options. (A) Har request pe Postgres `UPDATE usage_counters SET value = value + 1` -- durable aur accurate, lekin har tenant ki ek hi row pe har request ka update = hot row contention (row lock serialisation), WAL volume, aur request latency mein DB write. Busy tenant pe yeh khud bottleneck. (B) Redis INCR + periodic flush (mera choice) -- hot path ek O(1) INCR (pipeline with EXPIRE), Postgres pe har 60s ek upsert per counter. Cost: Redis loss pe up to ek flush interval ke counts lost, aur quota Redis pe enforced hai toh Redis reset = quota reset. TRADEOFFS #8. (C) Har request ka usage event stream (Kafka) mein, downstream aggregation (ClickHouse/warehouse) -- accurate, auditable, replayable; lekin infra heavy, aur enforcement ke liye phir bhi fast counter chahiye. SYSTEM_DESIGN.md 100x pe yahi suggest karta hai.

Decision factors: is project ka metering abhi quota enforcement aur visibility ke liye hai, invoice generation ke liye nahi (billing mock hai, flat plans). Approximate-but-cheap theek hai. Agar usage-based pricing ('Rs X per 1000 calls') aaye toh accuracy requirement badal jaati hai -- tab (C) ya (B) + durable event log. Flush ko idempotent banane ke liye absolute value + GREATEST -- delta-based nahi -- taaki duplicate ya concurrent flushes safe hon.

Senior point: enforcement path aur billing path ko alag karo. Enforcement fast aur approximate ho sakta hai (soft limits, thoda over allow); billing slow aur exact hona chahiye.
why_needed: Write-heavy metering design senior system design rounds ka common topic hai.
real_world_analogy: Cricket match ka scoreboard operator (Redis) har ball pe turant update karta hai; official scorer (Postgres) har over ke baad register mein likhta hai; aur ball-by-ball commentary recording (stream) se kabhi bhi poora match reconstruct ho sakta hai.
how_it_works: Hot path: INCR. Background: SCAN + upsert GREATEST. Future: events -> stream -> aggregates; counters only for enforcement.
follow_up_questions: Usage-based pricing aaye toh kya badloge?
Flush interval ka trade-off?
Exactly-once usage events kaise?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Accuracy vs cost vs complexity; B beech ka point hai jab enforcement primary goal ho.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Redis loss, worker down, month boundary, duplicate flush (safe due to GREATEST).
advanced.alternatives: Postgres hot-row (A); Kafka events (C); Postgres append-only usage_events table with periodic rollup (B'); provider-side metered billing.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x: B still fine with batch flush. 100x: C with per-tenant partitioned topics; counters sharded.
advanced.production_improvements: Seed counters from DB on Redis miss, flush lag metrics, durable event log for billing, reconciliation reports.

question: Explicit cache invalidation plus TTL: why both, and what are the gaps?
answer_hinglish:
Explicit invalidation freshness deta hai hamare apne writes ke baad: project create/delete pe `projects:list` delete, role change/remove pe `member-role:{user}` delete, billing webhook aur admin status change pe `_global` `tenant-slug:{slug}` delete. Isse 'maine project banaya aur list mein nahi dikha' jaisi UX problems nahi aati -- `test_tenant_aware_cache_never_crosses_tenants` create ke baad list 2 items assert karta hai, `test_platform_admin_suspension` suspend ke turant baad 403.

TTL (60s) safety net hai: (1) invalidation miss ho jaye (Redis error swallowed, race), (2) data app ke bahar badle -- manual SQL, migration, support script -- TRADEOFFS #11: 'changes made outside the app (manual SQL) appear after TTL', (3) koi code path invalidate karna bhool jaye. Dono milke: normal case mein fresh, worst case mein bounded staleness.

Gaps jo maine code mein dekhe: (1) Billing upgrade mein test explicitly `cache.invalidate('_global', 'tenant-slug:acme')` karta hai jab DB direct update karta hai -- out-of-band change ka example. (2) Stale-set race (read old -> invalidate -> set old). (3) `invalidate` failure silent. (4) Slug cache plan aur status dono rakhta hai -- plan change aur suspension dono isi key pe depend; invalidation `_invalidate_tenant_cache` pehle DB se slug padhta hai. (5) API key creator role cache nahi hota -- consistency over performance.

Alternatives: write-through (write ke saath cache update), versioned keys, change data capture (Postgres logical decoding -> invalidation events) jo out-of-band changes bhi pakde.
why_needed: Cache consistency strategy common question hai; 'TTL as safety net' ka reasoning chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Notice board: naya notice lagate hi purana hata dete ho (invalidation), aur har shaam saare notices hatake fresh lagate ho (TTL) taaki koi chhoota hua purana notice zyada din na rahe.
how_it_works: Write -> commit -> DEL keys. Read miss -> load -> SET EX ttl. Staleness <= TTL in failure cases.
in_this_project: `saas/services/cache.py::TenantCache` (`ttl`, `invalidate`), `saas/api/routes.py` (`create_project`, `delete_project`, `change_role`, `remove_member`, `_invalidate_tenant_cache`), TRADEOFFS.md #11, `tests/test_api.py::test_tenant_aware_background_job` (manual invalidate after direct DB update).
code_example:
# real tests/test_api.py (out-of-band change needs manual invalidation)
async with global_tx(sm) as s:
    await s.execute(text("UPDATE tenants SET plan = 'pro' WHERE id = :t"), {"t": t["id"]})
await c.app.state.cache.invalidate("_global", "tenant-slug:acme")
disadvantages: Out-of-band changes stale up to TTL

question: How do you deploy a schema change safely in this system, given the two roles and RLS?
answer_hinglish:
Deploy order DEPLOYMENT.md mein hai: 'Run migrations as a separate step before rolling the API.' docker-compose mein `migrate` service owner role se `alembic upgrade head` chalati hai aur `api`/`worker` `service_completed_successfully` pe depend karte hain. Production mein bhi: CI/CD pipeline mein migration job (owner credentials sirf is job ko), phir rolling deploy.

Nayi tenant table add karne ka checklist (RLS ki wajah se extra steps): (1) `tenant_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE`. (2) `ENABLE` + `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`. (3) `CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ... USING (...) WITH CHECK (...)` -- same strict predicate, no OR. (4) Tenant-first indexes. (5) `GRANT` to saas_app -- minimum (append-only tables pe sirf SELECT, INSERT); bhoole toh app ko 'permission denied'. (6) Sequence grants agar serial/identity. (7) SQL-level test: unfiltered query doosre tenant ki row nahi dekhti, cross-tenant insert fail. Bhoola hua policy step sabse khatarnak hai -- table bina RLS ke = no isolation backstop, aur koi error nahi aata.

Backward compatibility (rolling deploy mein purane aur naye pods saath chalte hain): expand/contract -- pehle additive changes (nullable column, new table), code deploy, backfill, phir constraints/removals agle release mein. Large table pe index `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (transaction ke bahar chalta hai -- alembic mein autocommit block chahiye). Policy change (jaise 0003) atomic hona chahiye: DROP POLICY aur CREATE POLICY ek transaction mein, warna beech mein table pe zero policies + RLS enabled = fail closed (zero rows) -- safe lekin outage. Postgres transactional DDL yahan help karta hai; alembic `context.begin_transaction()` mein migration chalata hai.
why_needed: Production deploys with security-critical schema (RLS) -- interviewer operational maturity dekhta hai.
real_world_analogy: Building mein naya kamra banana: pehle lock aur access rules (policy, grants), phir hi furniture aur log (data, code). Bina lock ke kamra kholna sabse bada risk.
how_it_works: Migrate (owner) -> verify -> roll app (saas_app). New table: tenant_id + ENABLE/FORCE + policy + indexes + grants + tests.
advantages: Transactional DDL makes policy swaps atomic
Owner credentials scoped to migration job
disadvantages: Manual checklist for RLS on new tables
common_mistakes: Non-concurrent index on large table (locks writes)
follow_up_questions: CI mein kaise check karoge ki har tenant table pe RLS hai?
Expand/contract ka example?
Migration rollback strategy?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Separate migration step safety aur clarity deta hai; cost yeh ki deploy pipeline mein ek stage aur backward-compat discipline.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Migration partially applied (non-transactional ops like CONCURRENTLY); new pods before migration -> errors; policy forgotten -> silent isolation gap.
advanced.alternatives: App-startup migrations (simpler, but app needs owner rights -- reject); schema management tools (Atlas, sqitch) with policy linting.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Silo/hybrid pe fleet-wide migrations orchestrated in waves; big tables pe online schema change tooling.
advanced.production_improvements: CI test: query pg_class for tables with tenant_id where relrowsecurity/relforcerowsecurity false -> fail; migration dry-run on prod-size copy; lock_timeout in migrations.
